_comment: Comparative knowledge for the Perazim Guide's drift detection. Status DRAFT_PENDING_LEVI: every entry is a summary written for review, not an approved source. Only the text in 'summary', 'origin' and 'scripture' is shown to the model. 'internal_note' is never shown to the model or to users. Scripture references are KJV and are retrieved verbatim from the bundled KJV database; no other translation is quoted. Entries are context only: the model may explain them but may not cite them. Standard: historic Protestant, Evangelical and Pentecostal orthodoxy, with Scripture as supreme authority. Under Levi's PR 76 correction, O-2 is superseded: the guide may name and accurately describe the Roman Catholic and Eastern Orthodox traditions from their own primary sources, and evaluates them from Scripture.

entries.summary: Karma, in Hindu, Buddhist and Jain teaching, is the principle that intentional actions bring results that shape later experience, including future lives. The three traditions explain karma differently. Jain teaching treats karma as a subtle matter that binds the soul, while Buddhist teaching describes karmic consequence without an eternal self.
entries.origin: Karma developed in Indian religious thought and is tied to rebirth and to the goal of release from it. Each tradition gives its own account of how karma works and what release requires.
entries.scripture: Scripture does not teach karma as a cosmic law of cause and rebirth. It teaches that it is appointed unto men once to die, and after this the judgment (Hebrews 9:27). Salvation is by grace through faith, not by the balance of deeds (Ephesians 2:8-9). Galatians 6:7-8 uses farming imagery about the harvest of living for the flesh or for the Spirit in this life. It is not a teaching of karma or of rebirth.

entries.summary: Reincarnation, or rebirth, is the teaching in several Indian traditions that a person or life-stream is reborn in new lives, with the next life shaped by karma. Hindu and Jain teaching hold that a self or soul continues through rebirths. Buddhist teaching denies an eternal self and explains rebirth as the continuation of a causal series of impermanent elements. Some New Age and esoteric writers also teach reincarnation.
entries.origin: Rebirth is central to Hindu and Jain teaching. Buddhist teaching denies a permanent self (anatta), so rebirth is explained by causal continuity, not by an eternal soul passing from body to body.
entries.scripture: Scripture teaches that it is appointed unto men once to die, and after this the judgment (Hebrews 9:27). Jesus told the thief on the cross, 'To day shalt thou be with me in paradise' (Luke 23:43), and Paul wrote of his desire 'to depart, and to be with Christ' (Philippians 1:23). These passages describe life with Christ after death, not a return to earth. The Christian view is that reincarnation is not taught in Scripture.

entries.summary: Nirvana in Buddhism and moksha in Hindu traditions are goals of release, and the traditions define them differently. Buddhist nirvana is release from craving and suffering, understood through the teaching of no permanent self. Moksha is liberation from rebirth, and Hindu schools describe it in different ways. In Jain teaching, liberation is the complete removal of karmic matter from the self.
entries.origin: Nirvana and moksha are goals of practice in Buddhist, Hindu and Jain traditions. Each is explained on its own terms and should not be reduced to a single idea of liberating the self.
entries.scripture: Scripture does not describe release from rebirth. It presents eternal life as the gift of God through his Son (John 3:16) and the hope of being with the Lord (2 Corinthians 5:8). Jesus said: 'I am the way, the truth, and the life: no man cometh unto the Father, but by me' (John 14:6). He also said: 'If the Son therefore shall make you free, ye shall be free indeed' (John 8:36).

entries.summary: Catholic teaching holds that purgatory is a final purification after death for those who die in God's grace but are still imperfectly purified, before they enter heaven. The Council of Trent, in its decree on purgatory, taught that the souls there are helped by the suffrages of the faithful. Eastern Orthodox teaching also prays for the departed, and its relation to the Catholic doctrine needs an official Orthodox source. Protestant and Evangelical Christians do not find purgatory taught in Scripture.
entries.origin: The Catholic doctrine developed in the medieval West and was defined at the Council of Trent (Session 25, December 1563). Its scriptural basis is disputed between its advocates and Protestant readers.
entries.scripture: Scripture says that the blood of Jesus Christ cleanses from all sin (1 John 1:7), and that believers are justified freely by his grace through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus (Romans 3:24). Paul says that to be absent from the body is to be present with the Lord (2 Corinthians 5:8). The Catechism's paragraph 1032 draws on 2 Maccabees 12:46, a book outside the Protestant canon, and 1 Corinthians 3:13-15 speaks of works tested by fire. Protestant readers take that passage to describe the testing and reward of Christian work at the judgment, not a post-death cleansing, and find no cleansing after death beyond the work of Christ.

entries.summary: Catholic teaching holds that departed saints, including Mary, pray for believers on earth, and that the faithful may ask them for intercession. It distinguishes this veneration of saints from the worship due to God alone. Some Eastern Orthodox writers also pray for the departed and hold that they intercede, but the official Orthodox position needs its own source. Protestant and Evangelical Christians hold that Christ alone is the mediator, and that prayer is addressed to God.
entries.origin: Asking the saints for intercession developed in Christian tradition after the New Testament period. Protestant teaching rejects it as going beyond Scripture.
entries.scripture: 1 Timothy 2:1-7 commands prayer and intercession for all people, and in the same passage says there is one God and one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus (1 Timothy 2:5). The disagreement is whether the intercession of departed saints belongs to that prayer. Hebrews 4:16 invites believers to come boldly to the throne of grace. Scripture does not show departed saints hearing or answering prayer, and Deuteronomy 18:10-12 forbids consulting the dead. Protestant readers hold that Christ's unique mediation does not stop believers praying for one another, but that prayer addressed to the departed would set up another mediator.

entries.summary: Catholic teaching honours Mary as Mother of God and, in its devotional and doctrinal tradition, uses titles such as mediatrix and queen of heaven. Co-redemptrix is a disputed title, and Catholic writers explain it in different ways. Eastern Orthodox teaching honours Mary as Theotokos, Mother of God, and does not hold her as co-redeemer. Protestant and Evangelical Christians hold that Jesus is the only mediator and redeemer.
entries.origin: These titles developed in later tradition and are not found in the New Testament. Queen of heaven has older devotional roots; mediatrix and co-redemptrix were developed later and are the most disputed.
entries.scripture: Scripture calls Mary blessed among women (Luke 1:42) and points people to her Son (John 2:5). Mary herself calls God her Saviour (Luke 1:47). Scripture names Jesus as the one mediator (1 Timothy 2:5) and the only Saviour who saves by his own work (Acts 4:12). Redemption is finished in Christ, and no one shares his office. Protestant readers honour Mary as the mother of the Lord and reject titles that give her a share in redemption or in the mediation of grace.
entries.internal_note: Catholic primary documents on the Marian titles and the Assumption (defined 1950) to be verified before release. Eastern Orthodox teaching on Theotokos and co-redemption to be verified against an Orthodox primary source.

entries.summary: Catholic and Eastern Orthodox traditions use icons, statues and prayer beads in devotion. Eastern Orthodox teaching defends the veneration of icons and distinguishes it from the worship due to God alone. Catholic teaching allows images and the veneration of saints through them. Many Protestant and Evangelical Christians, especially in Reformed traditions, hold that images used in worship, and bowing before them, are forbidden by the second commandment, while accepting images in teaching and art.
entries.origin: The controversy over icons in the eighth and ninth centuries was settled in favour of icon veneration by councils in the Eastern Church. Protestant teaching holds that this went beyond Scripture.
entries.scripture: The second commandment forbids making an image in order to bow down to it and serve it (Exodus 20:4-5). Scripture also records God's command to make cherubim for the mercy seat (Exodus 25:18-22), so the question is the use and veneration of images, not every image. Jesus said that the Father seeks true worshippers, who worship him in spirit and in truth (John 4:23-24). The Orthodox defence distinguishes the veneration of icons from the worship due to God. Protestant readers answer that Scripture gives no warrant for bowing to images as aids to worship.
entries.internal_note: Second Council of Nicaea (787) and Catholic teaching on images: primary text pending. Eastern Orthodox official teaching on icons: pending.

entries.summary: Soul sleep is the teaching that the dead are unconscious until the resurrection. Christadelphian teaching states that all await resurrection in the sleep of death, where there is no consciousness. Seventh-day Adventist Fundamental Belief 26 states that until that day death is an unconscious state for all people. Historic Catholic, Orthodox, Protestant and Evangelical teaching holds that believers are conscious with the Lord at death.
entries.origin: Soul sleep is taught in Christadelphian and Seventh-day Adventist publications. It departs from the historic majority view, which holds that the soul continues conscious after death.
entries.scripture: Ecclesiastes 9:5 says: 'For the living know that they shall die: but the dead know not any thing,' and advocates of soul sleep cite it with Daniel 12:2 for the dead who awake. Those who hold that the dead are conscious cite Luke 16:19-31, the rich man and Lazarus, which is a parable and must be read by its genre; Philippians 1:20-23, which speaks of departing to be with Christ; and 2 Corinthians 5:6-8, which speaks of being absent from the body and present with the Lord. Luke 23:43 is read in more than one way because the earliest Greek manuscripts have no punctuation, so it is strongest set beside these other passages. Protestant and Evangelical readers conclude that the dead are not unconscious, and that the resurrection of the body is the future completion of the hope.

entries.summary: Conditional immortality teaches that immortality is given only to those who receive eternal life in Christ, and is not an inherent property of the soul. It holds that those who reject God are destroyed rather than suffering conscious punishment for ever. The traditional Christian view holds that the lost suffer conscious punishment for ever. Perazim has not approved a position on the nature or duration of final punishment, so the guide sets out both views and does not state one as Perazim's.
entries.origin: Conditional immortality is taught in some Jehovah's Witness, Seventh-day Adventist and Christadelphian publications, and has been held by some evangelical scholars. The traditional view is the historic position of the Catholic and Eastern Orthodox churches and of most Protestant and Evangelical churches.
entries.scripture: Advocates of conditional immortality cite 1 Timothy 6:16, which says that God alone hath immortality; Romans 6:23, that eternal life is God's gift; and Ezekiel 18:4, that the soul that sinneth shall die. Advocates of the traditional view cite Matthew 25:46, where the same word for eternal describes both the life of the righteous and the punishment of the wicked, and Revelation 20:10, which describes the devil, the beast and the false prophet being tormented day and night for ever. Revelation 20:10 names those three and cannot, by itself, settle the fate of every person. The guide explains both arguments and does not decide between them for Perazim.

entries.summary: Religious pluralism is the view, held in several forms, that the religions are valid ways of approaching a reality no one religion has fully grasped. Philosophical pluralists hold that the religions point imperfectly to one ultimate reality. Radical pluralists hold that the religions are irreducibly diverse. Pluralism is not the teaching of Hinduism as a whole, or of every New Age writer. Christians hold that Jesus Christ is the one way to the Father.
entries.origin: Pluralism is a modern philosophical view, shaped by the comparative study of religions and held in different forms.
entries.scripture: Jesus said: 'I am the way, the truth, and the life: no man cometh unto the Father, but by me' (John 14:6). Peter said that there is no other name under heaven given among men by which we must be saved (Acts 4:12). These claims are exclusive, so the Christian reading does not allow that all religions lead to the same salvation. Scripture also teaches that God is known in part through creation (Romans 1:20). Christians may recognise truth and goodness in other traditions while holding that salvation is in Christ alone.

sources.title: David Basinger, Religious Diversity (Pluralism), Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy (2004, rev. 2025)

entries.summary: Advaita Vedanta, a school of Hindu philosophy associated with Shankara, teaches that the individual self (atman) is numerically identical with Brahman, the ultimate reality, and that liberation is the recognition of this nonduality. Other Hindu schools, including Dvaita and Vishishtadvaita, describe the relation between self and God differently and do not teach that the self is God. Some New Age writing says that people are divine by nature.
entries.origin: The identity of atman and Brahman is a central teaching of the Upanishads as interpreted in Advaita Vedanta. Hindu traditions vary in their account of Brahman.
entries.scripture: Scripture teaches that God created humans in his image (Genesis 1:27), and that the Creator is distinct from his creation (Isaiah 40:25; Romans 1:25). Humans are not God. Jesus is the eternal Son who is God (John 1:1; Colossians 2:9), and believers are adopted as children of God by grace (Galatians 4:5).

entries.summary: Latter-day Saint teaching distinguishes salvation from exaltation. The Church's essay Becoming Like God describes exaltation as the full inheritance of a child of God, available through the Atonement of Jesus Christ and by obedience to the laws and ordinances of the gospel, and says that the power of the Atonement is accessed through faith, repentance, baptism, the gift of the Holy Ghost and enduring to the end. The essay quotes the couplet 'As man now is, God once was: As God now is, man may be', and says that little has been revealed about its first half and that little is taught about it today.
entries.origin: The teaching of exaltation and of becoming like God comes from Joseph Smith and later Latter-day Saint leaders. The essay says that what the early church fathers meant by becoming God is open to interpretation, and that the biblical passages on human divine potential can be read in different ways.
entries.scripture: Scripture says there is one God, and that none was formed before or after him (Isaiah 43:10). God is not a man, that he should lie (Numbers 23:19). Believers are called children of God and heirs with Christ (Romans 8:16-17), and salvation is the free gift of God through Jesus Christ our Lord (Romans 6:23). Scripture says believers are to be conformed to the image of the Son (Romans 8:29). Protestant and Evangelical teaching holds that this is conformity to Christ in holiness and glory, and not becoming gods. The guide explains the Latter-day Saint teaching in its own terms before evaluating it.

entries.summary: Groups differ on how works relate to salvation, so each position is described separately. Latter-day Saint teaching holds that salvation is through the grace of Christ and that exaltation depends on obedience to the gospel's laws and ordinances. The Book of Mormon says it is 'by grace that we are saved, after all we can do' (2 Nephi 25:23). Jehovah's Witness teaching holds that salvation is God's undeserved kindness, that works prove living faith but do not earn salvation, and that a person who stops exercising faith could lose it. Many world religions teach that deeds affect liberation or future lives, each in its own terms.
entries.origin: These positions are distinct and should not be grouped together as one doctrine.
entries.scripture: Scripture says: 'For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God: Not of works, lest any man should boast' (Ephesians 2:8-9). Paul writes that a man is justified by faith without the deeds of the law (Romans 3:28). Good works are the fruit of salvation and the evidence of living faith (Ephesians 2:10; James 2:17-18). Protestant and Evangelical teaching holds that faith alone justifies, and that the faith which justifies produces works. The Christian question for Jehovah's Witness teaching is whether the obedience they require is fruit of grace or a condition the believer must still meet to keep salvation.

entries.summary: In many African traditional religions, the dead who lived well are remembered as ancestors who remain part of the family and community. Scholars describe veneration and reverence as the usual terms, rather than worship, and note that ancestral spirits are consulted on important occasions. Practices differ between peoples, regions and families, and some communities also recognise a supreme God. The guide distinguishes honouring and remembering the dead from invoking, consulting or making offerings to them, and does not generalise one practice across African peoples.
entries.origin: African traditional religions are many systems, not one. The SAGE Encyclopedia of African Religion (2009) calls the veneration of ancestors a fundamental part of African religion, while noting both shared patterns and variation. Community-specific accounts should be consulted before release.
entries.scripture: Scripture commands honour for parents (Exodus 20:12) and names Christ as the one mediator (1 Timothy 2:5). It forbids divination, consulting familiar spirits and inquiring of the dead (Deuteronomy 18:10-12), so Christians distinguish honouring and remembering family from seeking guidance or mediation from them. Christian prayer and worship are addressed to the triune God, and Christ is addressed in prayer as well (Acts 7:59; 1 Corinthians 1:2). Christians may honour and remember family members without seeking their intercession, and Deuteronomy 18 is not to be used to condemn every act of cultural respect.

entries.summary: Three groups reject the Trinity in different ways. Oneness Pentecostal teaching holds that God is one person who reveals himself as Father, Son and Holy Spirit in different manifestations or roles; Trinitarian theologians often call this modalism, though Oneness adherents may reject that label. Jehovah's Witness teaching holds that the Son is a created being and the Holy Spirit is God's impersonal active force. Latter-day Saint teaching holds that the Father, Son and Holy Ghost are three separate beings who make up the Godhead.
entries.origin: These are separate positions, each described from its own published teaching. Historic Christian orthodoxy, including Catholic, Eastern Orthodox, Protestant, Evangelical and Pentecostal churches, affirms one God in three persons.
entries.scripture: Deuteronomy 6:4 teaches the oneness of God: 'Hear, O Israel: The LORD our God is one LORD.' The Father, Son and Holy Spirit are named together in the baptismal commission (Matthew 28:19). Against Oneness teaching, Scripture shows the Father and the Son as distinct persons who speak to each other (John 17:5) and the Son who is sent by the Father, who sends the Spirit (John 14:16-17, 26), alongside the passages affirming the deity of the Son (John 1:1; Hebrews 1:8). Against Jehovah's Witness teaching, the Son is called God (John 1:1; Hebrews 1:8) and the Spirit is a person who teaches, can be grieved and can be lied to (John 14:26; Ephesians 4:30; Acts 5:3-4). Against Latter-day Saint teaching, historic Christianity holds that God is one in essence and three in persons, not three separate beings.

entries.summary: Jehovah's Witness teaching identifies Jesus with the archangel Michael and holds that Jesus is a created being, not the eternal God the Son. The Jehovah's Witness page on Michael says that Michael is evidently a name given to Jesus before and after his life on earth, and that both names refer to the same person. Historic Nicene Christianity rejects this identification and affirms the eternal deity of the Son.
entries.origin: This is Jehovah's Witness teaching. It rests on that group's reading of Daniel 10:13, Jude 9, 1 Thessalonians 4:16 and related passages.
entries.scripture: Scripture says that Jesus is the eternal Word who was God (John 1:1-3), that all things were created by him (Colossians 1:16), and that he is the image of the invisible God (Colossians 1:15). Hebrews 1:5 asks: 'Unto which of the angels said he at any time, Thou art my Son?' Hebrews 1:6 says that God commands all the angels to worship him. Jehovah's Witness readers take Jude 9 and 1 Thessalonians 4:16 to identify Michael as the archangel and as Jesus. Jude 9 does not itself say that Michael is not Jesus, so the identification rests on the wider argument, which Hebrews 1 answers.

He is called God (Acts 5:3-4). The Holy Spirit is also one of the three persons named in the baptismal commission (Matthew 28:19).

entries.summary: Latter-day Saint teaching includes baptism for the dead, a proxy ordinance in which a living person is baptised on behalf of someone who has died. The Church's topic essay says the ordinance is an offer, and that the validity of a proxy baptism depends on the deceased person accepting it. The Church cites 1 Corinthians 15:29 as evidence that baptisms for the dead were done in Paul's time.
entries.origin: This is a Latter-day Saint practice performed in temples. The Church's doctrinal basis is that God has prepared a way for all people to receive the blessings of baptism.
entries.scripture: Scripture teaches that people believe and are baptised in this life in response to the gospel (Mark 16:16; Acts 2:38). In 1 Corinthians 15:29 Paul mentions baptism for the dead without commending the practice or giving a command to follow it. Its meaning is disputed among commentators, so it cannot bear the weight of a doctrine. Mark 16:9-20 is a passage whose authenticity is disputed, so Mark 16:16 is not the main proof. Hebrews 9:27 says that after death comes the judgment, and Protestant and Evangelical teaching holds that salvation is received by faith in this life.

sources.title: Baptisms for the Dead, Gospel Topics (LDS, Topics and Questions 2023)
sources.use: proxy baptism offered; validity depends on the deceased person accepting; the Church cites 1 Corinthians 15:29

entries.summary: Seventh-day Adventists keep the seventh day, Saturday, as the Sabbath. Their Fundamental Belief 20 requires observance of the seventh-day Sabbath as the day of rest, worship and ministry, and Fundamental Belief 13 describes the remnant as keeping the commandments of God and the faith of Jesus. Their Biblical Research Institute materials place Sunday observance within the end-time test over worship, in which Sunday is presented as the mark of allegiance to the beast. The guide does not say that present-day Sunday worshippers are condemned or bear the mark.
entries.origin: This is Seventh-day Adventist teaching on the Sabbath and the end-time test. Most Christians worship on the first day of the week, the day of the resurrection.
entries.scripture: Colossians 2:16-17 says: 'Let no man therefore judge you in meat, or in drink, or in respect of an holyday, or of the new moon, or of the sabbath days.' Romans 14:5-6 says that each should be fully persuaded in his own mind, and that he who observes the day observes it unto the Lord. Adventist readers rely on Revelation 14:12, which speaks of those who keep the commandments of God, and on the seventh-day Sabbath as the sign of loyalty. Protestant and Evangelical readers hold that the Sabbath is not a binding requirement for Christians, that Christ is Lord of the Sabbath (Mark 2:28), and that the early church gathered on the first day (Acts 20:7; 1 Corinthians 16:2).

entries.summary: New Age teaching is a diverse movement, not one doctrine. Britannica describes it as a body of diverse believers united by a few ideas, with strongest roots in modern esotericism and in Helena Blavatsky's Theosophical Society. Its ideas include healing and self-transformation, daily group meditation, and an expected age of heightened spiritual consciousness. Some writers teach that people shape reality by focused thought; that idea should be treated as a separate strand and sourced separately.
entries.origin: The movement draws on Theosophy and modern esotericism, and on concepts from Hindu and Buddhist traditions. Its strands differ in origin, and they should not be presented as one teaching.
entries.scripture: Scripture teaches that God is Spirit (John 4:24) and is personal, not an impersonal energy, and that creation is his. Healing is sought from God in prayer (James 5:14-15), and God's purposes are not determined by human thought or manifestation. Believers are told to test every spirit (1 John 4:1). Scripture forbids divination and the seeking of guidance from the occult (Deuteronomy 18:10-12).

entries.summary: Christian Science, founded by Mary Baker Eddy, affirms the crucifixion and resurrection of Jesus and the divinity of the Christ. Its official tenets say that the crucifixion and resurrection served to uplift faith to understand eternal Life. Its FAQ says that, while it affirms the divinity of the Christ, it does not equate Jesus with God. It teaches that matter is nothing and that healing comes through understanding God as Mind. Christian Scientists are free to choose their own healthcare, and the FAQ says they may visit doctors.
entries.origin: Christian Science was founded by Mary Baker Eddy, whose main text, Science and Health with Key to the Scriptures, was first published in 1875.
entries.scripture: Scripture describes Jesus as a real man who was born, suffered, died and rose bodily (Luke 24:39; 1 Corinthians 15:3-4). The Son is God (John 1:1; Colossians 2:9). Christian faith takes the incarnation, the crucifixion and the resurrection as physical and historical events. Christian healing is by God's power through prayer and faith (James 5:14-16), and Scripture does not teach that matter is nothing. The atonement is by the blood of Christ (Ephesians 1:7). The guide describes Christian Science's own interpretation before evaluating it.

entries.summary: Secular and non-religious worldviews differ, and the guide describes the specific one a person holds. Atheism is the view that God does not exist. Agnosticism is not one claim. In one sense an agnostic believes neither that theism nor that atheism is true; in another, the agnostic holds that neither theism nor atheism is known. Scientific naturalism holds that nature is all there is. Secular humanism bases ethics on reason and human welfare rather than revelation. Secular thinkers disagree about morality: some defend objective moral values and others do not.
entries.origin: Atheism, agnosticism, naturalism, secular humanism and related views have different histories and should not be treated as one position. The Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy distinguishes the psychological and epistemological senses of agnosticism, and notes that atheism and metaphysical naturalism are not identical.
entries.scripture: Psalm 19:1 says that the heavens declare the glory of God. Psalm 14:1 says 'The fool hath said in his heart, There is no God,' and in the poem the word describes a moral and spiritual condition, not a philosophical argument. The guide does not use the verse as an insult to any questioner. Romans 1:19-20 says that God's invisible power and nature are clearly seen through creation, and Romans 2:14-15 says that the law is written on human hearts. Faith and reason are not opposed, and Acts 17:11 commends those who searched the Scriptures to test what they heard.

entries.summary: Islamic teaching, based on the Qur'an, holds that Jesus was neither killed nor crucified, and that the crucifixion only appeared to happen. Muslim scholars read the verse in more than one way. A prominent reading holds that someone else was made to resemble Jesus, and other readings differ from it. The guide describes this teaching in its own words and does not quote the Qur'an.
entries.origin: The teaching rests on Surah 4:157 and its interpretation in Muslim tradition. A 2023 article in the American Journal of Islam and Society reviews the long-standing view that the verse denies the crucifixion and defends that reading from context and language.
entries.scripture: The New Testament reports that Jesus was crucified and died (Matthew 27:50; Acts 2:23), and that he rose from the dead (1 Corinthians 15:3-4). Paul calls the message Christ crucified (1 Corinthians 1:23). The Roman historian Tacitus also reports the execution of Christ under Pontius Pilate (Annals 15.44). The Christian response engages both the historical evidence and the theological claim.

entries.summary: Islamic teaching holds that God has no son and neither begets nor is begotten. Jesus, called the Messiah, is honoured as a prophet and messenger of God and as born of Mary, but he is not divine. Islam rejects the Christian confession that Jesus is the Son of God and the doctrine of the Trinity. The guide paraphrases these teachings and does not quote the Qur'an.
entries.origin: This is the teaching of Islam, based on the Qur'an. The Qur'an is paraphrased here, not quoted. The meaning of the relevant Surahs should be checked against the authorised translation and classical tafsir before release.
entries.scripture: Scripture teaches that Jesus is the eternal Son of God (John 1:14; Hebrews 1:2-3), that he is God (John 1:1; Titus 2:13), and that he is the one mediator between God and men (1 Timothy 2:5). Jesus said: 'I and my Father are one' (John 10:30). Christians hold that the Father's begetting of the Son is eternal and not physical, and that the Son's divinity is shown in his works, his resurrection and his own claims. Islam honours Jesus as Messiah and prophet while rejecting the Christian confession of his divine Sonship.

entries.summary: The Protestant and Evangelical Bible contains 66 books: 39 in the Old Testament and 27 in the New. The Catholic canon adds Old Testament books such as Tobit, Judith, Wisdom, Sirach, Baruch and 1 and 2 Maccabees. Eastern Orthodox canons are not one universal list. The Synod of Jerusalem's list includes 1 Esdras, 3 Maccabees, the Prayer of Manasseh, Psalm 151 and the Odes, and the Armenian and Ethiopian churches have further lists. The Westminster Confession states that the books commonly called Apocrypha are not of divine inspiration and form no part of the canon.
entries.origin: The 66-book canon was recognised through the church's reception of apostolic books and of the Old Testament books that Jesus and the apostles cited as Scripture. The Catholic canon was defined at the Council of Trent. Protestant Reformers returned to the shorter Hebrew canon. Lists differ across Christian history, and some boundaries were debated.
entries.scripture: Scripture is given by inspiration of God (2 Timothy 3:16), and Peter counts Paul's letters with the other Scriptures (2 Peter 3:15-16). Jesus and the apostles treated the Old Testament writings as Scripture, including the phrase 'the law of Moses, and the prophets, and the psalms' (Luke 24:44). That phrase names the divisions of the Hebrew Scriptures but does not itself list every book. Deuteronomy 4:2 and Revelation 22:18-19 warn against adding to or taking from God's words, but each passage is read in its own context and does not by itself fix the number of books. The Protestant view is that the 66 books are the inspired canon, and the additional books are read for history and edification.

entries.summary: A question asks whether a named church or group is true, saved, or a cult. The guide describes that institution's official, publicly documented teaching accurately and evaluates it against Scripture. Where an institution's official teaching contradicts Scripture and historic orthodox Christianity, the guide says so plainly, explains the contradiction and its doctrinal consequences. The guide does not decide the salvation of any individual adherent, does not assign guilt to members, and does not use the word cult as an unsupported label.
entries.origin: Policy entry. It governs how the guide answers questions about named churches and movements, and it does not express a doctrine.
entries.scripture: Scripture is the standard for every teaching (Isaiah 8:20; Acts 17:11). The guide tests an institution's official teaching against Scripture, so that a clear contradiction of Scripture is named as such. The judgment of any person's heart belongs to God (1 Samuel 16:7; Romans 14:12), so the guide does not decide any individual's eternal destiny.

entries.summary: A question names a religious group, such as Latter-day Saints, Jehovah's Witnesses, Seventh-day Adventists, Oneness Pentecostals, Christian Science, Christadelphians, the Catholic Church or the Eastern Orthodox churches. The guide describes the group's official teaching from its own published sources. It keeps apart official teaching, historical teaching, local practice and individual belief, and then evaluates the official teaching against Scripture. Catholic and Eastern Orthodox churches affirm the Nicene Trinity and historic Christology, and their differences from the Perazim framework are stated specifically.
entries.origin: Policy entry applying the group-specific entries. Each group's self-description comes from a primary source, with a scholarly source where needed.
entries.scripture: The guide explains each group's teaching in plain words, names the passages each side relies on, and shows what Scripture teaches (Acts 17:11; 1 John 4:1). It separates an institution's official teaching from local practice and individual belief, and it gives no verdict on any member's eternal destiny.
